 Interest Limitation on Loans from a Foreign Parent: The 30% of EBITDA Rule Explained for Indian Subsidiaries
 Sudheer 
 Sudheer 
 Author 
 Follow 
 View profile 
 Last updated: 21 November 2026 
 Save 
 Share 
 Join Us 
 Follow Us 
 Add as Source 
 When a foreign parent funds its Indian subsidiary with debt rather than equity, the interest paid back to the parent reduces Indian taxable profit. To stop excessive debt-funded profit shifting, Indian tax law contains an interest limitation rule based on OECD BEPS Action 4, originally introduced as section 94B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and carried into the Income-tax Act, 2025. With the 2026 liberalisation of the ECB framework making parent loans easier, this rule is now the main constraint on how much intercompany debt is tax-efficient.
 When the rule applies
 The borrower is an Indian company, or a permanent establishment of a foreign company in India.
 It pays interest or similar consideration on debt to a non-resident associated enterprise, or on debt from a third-party lender that is guaranteed or funded by an associated enterprise.
 The interest or similar expense exceeds INR 1 crore in the year.
 Banks and insurance businesses are outside the rule, and certain notified finance companies have been carved out.
 How the disallowance is computed
 The deductible interest is capped at 30% of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA). Only the interest paid or payable to the associated enterprise (or on guaranteed debt) is disallowed, and the disallowance is the lower of the total such interest and the excess of total interest over 30% of EBITDA.
 Item 
 INR crore 
 EBITDA 
 20.00 
 30% of EBITDA 
 6.00 
 Total interest expense (including INR 7 crore to the parent) 
 9.00 
 Excess interest over 30% of EBITDA 
 3.00 
 Disallowance (lower of 3.00 and 7.00) 
 3.00 
 The disallowed INR 3 crore can be carried forward for up to eight assessment years and deducted in a later year to the extent there is headroom within 30% of that year's EBITDA.
 Interaction with other rules
 Transfer pricing comes first: the interest rate and the quantum of debt must be at arm's length. Any transfer pricing adjustment reduces the interest before the 30% test is applied.
 Withholding tax: interest paid to the parent attracts withholding at domestic or treaty rates, regardless of whether part of it is disallowed.
 ECB conditions: FEMA end-use, maturity and reporting conditions apply independently of the tax rule.
 Equity alternatives: compulsorily convertible instruments are treated as equity under FEMA; whether their coupon is treated as interest for tax purposes needs separate analysis.
 Practical points for tax auditors and finance teams
 Compute EBITDA from the tax computation, not just the accounts, and document the working each year.
 Track carried-forward disallowances by year so they are not lost.
 Identify guarantees given by the parent for bank loans; interest on those loans can also fall within the rule.
 Model the rule before choosing between debt and equity for a capital-intensive subsidiary in its early, low-EBITDA years, where the cap bites hardest.
